practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a social care setting?
A) GP surgery
B) Walk-in centre
C) Residential home
D) Hospital
practice_questions.marks: C) Residential home [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one health care setting and one social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one health care setting (e.g. dental practice, GP surgery, hospital, nursing home, opticians, pharmacy, walk-in centre, health centre) AND one social care setting (e.g. residential home, community centre, foodbank, day centre, retirement home, homeless shelter, social services department, support group). Both must be correctly categorised to earn the mark.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the right to consultation in a health or social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that service users are involved in decisions about their own care; 1 mark for a brief qualifying detail (e.g. care plans are discussed with the service user before changes are made; the service user's views are sought and considered).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a GP surgery could uphold two of the five rights of its service users.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per right described. Accept any two rights with relevant application to a GP surgery setting. Example responses: Right to confidentiality (2 marks) -- 1 mark for identifying the right; 1 mark for a specific feature of a GP surgery (e.g. patient medical records are stored securely and only shared with clinicians who need them; a receptionist does not discuss a patient's appointment reason in a crowded waiting area). Right to choice (2 marks) -- 1 mark for identifying the right; 1 mark for a specific feature (e.g. a patient chooses between two treatment options discussed with their GP; a patient selects a preferred appointment time). Other rights awarded on the same principle: consultation, equal and fair treatment, or protection from abuse and harm, each with a GP surgery-specific example.

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important for service users in a residential care home to have their right to choice upheld.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the right to choice (e.g. residents can make decisions about their own care and daily life); 1 mark for a reason using 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that' (e.g. because it means they feel in control of their own lives); 1 mark for a further developed reason or consequence (e.g. therefore their emotional wellbeing is supported and they are less likely to feel powerless or lose their sense of identity).

practice_questions.text:
Fatima is a Healthcare Assistant on a 20-bed elderly care ward in an NHS hospital. One of her service users is Mr Okeke, a 78-year-old man who has recently been admitted following a fall. Mr Okeke speaks limited English and has a visual impairment.

Explain how the ward team could uphold three of the five rights for Mr Okeke during his stay. In your answer, refer to his specific circumstances.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies three rights clearly and links each to Mr Okeke's specific circumstances (limited English, visual impairment, hospital setting). Uses correct terminology throughout. Provides a clear chain of reasoning for each right using language such as 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that'. Example content -- right to consultation: the ward team should involve Mr Okeke in decisions about his treatment and discharge plan, therefore he feels respected and his care is tailored to his needs, even if this requires extra time or an interpreter. Right to equal and fair treatment: Mr Okeke must receive the same standard of pain management and clinical care as any other patient, because his language difference and visual impairment should not lead to assumptions about his preferences or capacity. Right to confidentiality: his medical information should not be shared with family members without his consent, even if they visit, because this respects his autonomy and builds trust with the care team.

Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies at least two rights with generally accurate explanation and some application to Mr Okeke, but may lack development or miss one of his specific circumstances.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies rights correctly but explanation is descriptive rather than reasoned; limited reference to Mr Okeke's circumstances.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a right with little or no explanation or application to the scenario.

practice_questions.text:
Which benefit is most directly produced when a service user's right to choice is upheld?
A) Trust
B) Empowerment
C) Needs being met
D) Equal treatment
practice_questions.marks: B) Empowerment [1 mark]. Accept C (needs being met) with a brief justification if clearly reasoned, but B is the primary answer expected.

practice_questions.text: Identify one benefit to a service user's health and wellbeing when their rights are maintained.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: empowerment / feeling in control; high self-esteem / feeling valued or respected; needs being met / appropriate care received; trust / confidence in care received.

practice_questions.text: Outline how maintaining the right to confidentiality leads to the benefit of trust for a service user.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the link between confidentiality and trust (e.g. the service user knows their personal information is kept private); 1 mark for explaining the outcome (e.g. therefore they feel reassured and confident that the practitioner has their best interests in mind).

practice_questions.text: Describe two benefits a 14-year-old service user at a community mental health drop-in centre might experience when practitioners uphold their rights.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per benefit, applied to the named setting and service user. Example: High self-esteem (2 marks) -- 1 mark for identifying the benefit; 1 mark for applying it to the young person in a community mental health setting (e.g. when the support worker treats her views with the same respect as any other attendee, she feels valued and respected, supporting positive mental health). Empowerment (2 marks) -- 1 mark for identifying the benefit; 1 mark for a setting-specific application (e.g. being consulted about her support goals means she feels in control of her own recovery, encouraging her to engage with the service). Other benefits (trust, needs met) accepted on the same principle.

practice_questions.text: Explain why maintaining the right to equal and fair treatment produces the benefit of high self-esteem for a service user in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the right and the benefit (equal and fair treatment leads to high self-esteem); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' (e.g. because the service user is not discriminated against or treated differently based on their characteristics, they feel valued and respected); 1 mark for extending the reasoning to a wellbeing outcome (e.g. this means that their positive mental health is supported and they are more likely to engage actively with their care).

practice_questions.text:
Stefan works as a key worker at Greenfields Day Centre, a social care setting for adults with learning disabilities. He supports David, a 29-year-old service user who attends four days a week. Stefan consistently asks David which activities he wants to take part in, involves David in reviews of his support plan and ensures David's dietary preferences are always catered for.

Discuss the benefits to David's health and wellbeing when his rights are maintained in this way. Refer to the specific rights being upheld in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Identifies multiple benefits and links each clearly to a specific right Stefan is upholding. Uses David's circumstances (learning disability, day centre, specific actions Stefan takes) to anchor the discussion. Develops a reasoning chain for each benefit and reaches a clear, supported judgement about the overall importance of rights-maintenance for David's wellbeing. Accurate use of terminology throughout (empowerment, self-esteem, trust, needs met). Example content: right to choice/consultation -> empowerment (David feels in control of his own day, therefore his independence and self-reliance are supported, this means that his emotional wellbeing and sense of identity are maintained). Right to choice/equal treatment -> needs being met (catering for dietary preferences means David's physical health is maintained and he is not malnourished or excluded at mealtimes). Right to consultation -> high self-esteem (being involved in his support plan reviews means David feels valued and respected, therefore his self-esteem is positive and he engages more openly with his care). Discussion should acknowledge that all four benefits are interconnected and that consistently upholding rights produces compounding positive effects on physical, emotional and social wellbeing.

Secure (5-6 marks): Identifies at least two benefits with mostly accurate explanations and reasonable application to David's situation. Links to rights present but may lack full development or judgement.

Developing (3-4 marks): Identifies benefits but explanation is descriptive; limited application to David specifically; limited use of 'because/therefore' reasoning.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Names one or two benefits with little explanation or application to the scenario.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the nine person-centred values?
A) Compassion
B) Competence
C) Privacy
D) Safeguarding
practice_questions.marks: C) Privacy [1 mark]. (Compassion and Competence are 6Cs, not person-centred values; safeguarding is Topic Area 4 content.)

practice_questions.text: Identify two person-centred values that a practitioner should apply when supporting a service user to make decisions about their care.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two values clearly relevant to decision making. Acceptable answers: choice and encouraging decision making; partnership and choice; independence and encouraging decision making. Both must be named correctly and be genuine values from the list of nine.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the person-centred value of dignity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the core meaning (treating service users with respect for their worth as a person, without humiliation or shame); 1 mark for a qualifying detail or brief example (e.g. using a calm professional manner during personal care; not using patronising language with older service users).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a domiciliary carer visiting an older adult at home could apply two person-centred values during their visit.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per value, applied to the domiciliary care context. Example: Dignity (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the value; 1 mark for a specific domiciliary care action and its impact (e.g. closing the front door before discussing the service user's medication means the service user is not overheard by neighbours and feels respected). Independence (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the value; 1 mark for a specific action (e.g. encouraging the service user to make their own breakfast with adapted equipment, rather than doing it for them, maintains their physical capability and self-esteem). Other values accepted on the same principle with relevant domiciliary care examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain why applying the person-centred value of respect is important for a service user in a residential care home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for defining or identifying the value of respect (recognising the service user's background, beliefs, culture and preferences); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' or 'therefore' (e.g. because the resident feels their identity and culture are valued by staff); 1 mark for a developed outcome (e.g. therefore they are more likely to engage honestly with their care team and their emotional wellbeing is supported).

practice_questions.text:
Bea is a support worker at Millbrook Day Centre, which supports adults aged 18-65 with learning disabilities. One of her service users, 24-year-old Kofi, has recently joined the centre and has limited verbal communication. He uses picture cards to express his preferences.

Explain how Bea could apply person-centred values when supporting Kofi during a day at the centre. Refer to specific values in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Identifies at least three specific person-centred values by name and explains clearly how Bea could apply each one in the context of Kofi's specific circumstances (learning disability, limited verbal communication, picture cards, day centre). Uses 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that' to develop reasoning chains. Example content: Individuality -- Bea learns Kofi's preferred communication method (picture cards) and uses them consistently, because this treats him as a unique person rather than assuming a generic approach will work, therefore Kofi feels recognised and understood. Choice -- Bea offers Kofi picture cards showing the morning's activities so he can select what he wants to do, this means that his right to make his own decisions is actively supported. Encouraging decision making -- Bea uses open picture-based questions to help Kofi build confidence in expressing preferences, because this develops his capacity to make choices over time. Dignity -- Bea speaks to Kofi directly, not about him to other staff, because this preserves his sense of worth. Partnership -- Bea involves Kofi in reviewing what support he needs each morning.

Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies at least two values with mostly accurate explanation and some reference to Kofi's circumstances.

Developing (2 marks): Names values but explanation is descriptive; limited specific application to Kofi.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a value with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the 6Cs?
A) Individuality
B) Compassion
C) Partnership
D) Dignity
practice_questions.marks: B) Compassion [1 mark]. (Individuality, Partnership and Dignity are person-centred values, not 6Cs.)

practice_questions.text: Name two of the 6Cs.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming two of the 6Cs: Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage, Commitment. Both must be from this list. Do not accept person-centred values such as dignity or respect.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the quality of competence in a health or social care practitioner.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the core meaning (having the knowledge, skills and ability to carry out professional duties safely and to the required standard); 1 mark for a qualifying detail (e.g. knowing when you are outside your competence and need to refer to a colleague or supervisor; having up-to-date training to perform tasks correctly).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a healthcare assistant on a hospital ward could demonstrate two of the 6Cs when supporting an elderly service user.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per 6C. Example: Compassion (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the quality; 1 mark for a specific ward action and its effect (e.g. sitting at the service user's eye level and speaking gently when explaining their medication options, so that the service user feels understood and respected). Care (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the quality; 1 mark for a specific action (e.g. checking the service user's fluid intake and nutrition without being asked, noticing any deterioration and reporting it to the nurse in charge, so that the service user's physical wellbeing is actively promoted). Other 6Cs accepted with relevant ward examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the quality of courage is important for a practitioner working in a residential care home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the quality of courage and what it involves (willingness to challenge poor practice, speak up or report a concern); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' (e.g. because care homes support vulnerable older adults who may not be able to report poor practice themselves); 1 mark for a developed consequence (e.g. therefore without courage, poor practice goes unchallenged and service users' right to protection from abuse and harm is not upheld).

practice_questions.text:
Priya is a key worker at Sunfield Community Centre, which runs a daily drop-in service for adults experiencing homelessness. One of the service users, 41-year-old Marcus, has a history of mental health difficulties and has not engaged with any support service for several months. He has just walked in for the first time.

Explain how Priya could use the 6Cs when supporting Marcus during his first visit. In your answer, refer to specific qualities and link them to the person-centred values they enable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Names at least three 6Cs clearly, explains what Priya does as a result of each quality in the context of Marcus's specific circumstances (homelessness, mental health difficulties, first visit, community centre setting). Links each 6C to a person-centred value it enables. Uses reasoning chains with 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that'. Example content: Compassion -- Priya listens without interrupting and acknowledges how difficult things have been for Marcus, therefore he feels understood and his dignity is upheld, this means that he is more likely to engage with the support available. Communication -- Priya speaks calmly and uses straightforward language, avoiding clinical jargon, because Marcus may feel anxious and overwhelmed, so this means he can take in the information and feel reassured. Courage -- If Marcus mentions something concerning about his safety, Priya documents and reports it to her line manager even if she is not certain, because his right to protection from harm is her duty to uphold. Commitment -- Priya follows up on his next visit and ensures his support plan is reviewed, because consistent support is particularly important for someone who has disengaged in the past.

Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies at least two 6Cs with mostly accurate explanation and some application to Marcus's situation.

Developing (2 marks): Names qualities but explanation is descriptive; limited application to Marcus.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one quality with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a benefit for SERVICE PROVIDERS of applying person-centred values?
A) Standardisation of care
B) Improved quality of life for the service user
C) Improved job satisfaction
D) Developing their own strengths
practice_questions.marks: C) Improved job satisfaction [1 mark]. (A, B and D are benefits for service users.)

practice_questions.text: Identify one benefit for a service user when person-centred values are applied in their care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: standardisation of care (same quality of care whoever is on duty); improved quality of care (tailored to the individual's needs); maintained or improved quality of life (physical, emotional and social wellbeing); supported to develop their strengths (builds capability and confidence).

practice_questions.text: Outline how applying person-centred values enables the sharing of good practice between practitioners.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the link (person-centred values create a common framework/language that practitioners can use when communicating good practice); 1 mark for a qualifying detail (e.g. improvements in one area can be shared with partner organisations; innovations can be written up in supervision notes and adopted elsewhere).

practice_questions.text: Describe two benefits for service users at a community day centre when the practitioners consistently apply person-centred values.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per benefit. Example: Improved quality of care (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the benefit; 1 mark for a day-centre-specific application (e.g. a practitioner who applies individuality learns each service user's preferred communication style and cultural background, therefore the care plan is genuinely tailored to the individual and their needs are more effectively met). Supporting service users to develop their strengths (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the benefit; 1 mark for a day-centre example (e.g. a service user who is encouraged to lead an activity they are skilled at gains confidence and social skills, supporting their independence). Other benefits accepted with relevant day-centre examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain why applying the person-centred value of independence leads to improved quality of life for a service user in a residential home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the value and the benefit (independence leads to improved quality of life); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' (e.g. because the practitioner encourages the service user to carry out daily tasks for themselves using adapted equipment, rather than doing everything for them); 1 mark for a developed consequence (e.g. therefore the service user maintains physical capability and confidence for longer, this means that their emotional wellbeing is supported and their daily life has greater purpose and meaning).

practice_questions.text:
Chidi is the manager of Hawthorn House, a 25-bed residential home for older adults. She is reviewing the home's approach to person-centred values following a new member of staff joining the team. Chidi explains to the new staff member that applying person-centred values consistently benefits both the staff team and the residents.

Discuss the benefits of applying person-centred values for both service providers and service users at Hawthorn House. In your answer, link each benefit to a specific person-centred value.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Discusses benefits for both service providers and service users clearly. Links each benefit to a specific named person-centred value. Applies the discussion to Hawthorn House (residential home for older adults, 25-bed, new staff member context). Uses reasoning chains. Reaches a clear, supported judgement -- e.g. 'The most significant benefit overall is standardisation of care for residents, because it ensures no resident's experience is dependent on which staff member is rostered, therefore all 25 residents at Hawthorn House receive consistently respectful, person-centred care regardless of shift.' Example content for service providers: clear guidelines and standards -- applying the value of dignity means staff know exactly what is expected during personal care (close curtains, professional manner, never patronise), so new staff can be inducted quickly and performance assessed consistently. Improved job satisfaction -- applying partnership means staff co-produce care plans with residents and see the positive outcomes, which motivates them to remain in post and deliver high-quality care. Example content for service users: standardisation -- all residents receive the same dignified, person-centred care whether it is day or night shift. Developing strengths -- applying the value of independence means residents are encouraged to do as much for themselves as possible, maintaining physical ability and self-confidence. Discussion should acknowledge the interconnection: staff satisfaction leads to lower turnover, which benefits residents through continuity of relationships and care. Answer should end with a supported judgement about which benefit(s) are most significant.

Secure (5-6 marks): Discusses at least two benefits for each group with mostly accurate explanations and some linking to specific values and to Hawthorn House.

Developing (3-4 marks): Identifies benefits but explanation is largely descriptive; links to values present but underdeveloped; limited application to the residential home context.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Names one or two benefits with little explanation, limited link to values, little or no application to the setting.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a physical effect on a service user when person-centred values are not applied?
A) Feeling excluded from group activities
B) Loss of concentration during sessions
C) Dehydration due to not being offered regular fluids
D) Low self-esteem
practice_questions.marks: C) Dehydration due to not being offered regular fluids [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one emotional effect and one social effect that can result when person-centred values are not applied in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for an emotional effect (accept: depression; feeling upset; low self-esteem/feeling inadequate; anger/frustration; stress). 1 mark for a social effect (accept: feeling excluded; feeling lonely; lack of social interaction/poor social skills; becoming withdrawn).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a service user may develop depression if person-centred values are not applied in a residential home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: identification of a missing value or its absence (1) — e.g. dignity or individuality not applied; link to an emotional consequence (1) — service user feels disrespected, invisible or unwanted; further development using 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that' (1) — e.g. 'because the service user has no sense of being valued, they stop engaging with staff and activities, which leads to persistent low mood and depression'. Credit other valid chains.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a lack of person-centred values could affect the physical and intellectual wellbeing of a service user living in a nursing home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Physical (up to 2): relevant effect named (1) — e.g. malnutrition/illness because dietary needs are not treated as individual (1); development or second point (1) — e.g. dehydration if fluids not regularly offered, leading to UTIs or falls. Intellectual (up to 2): relevant effect named (1) — e.g. lack of mental stimulation or loss of concentration; development linking to the nursing home context (1) — e.g. if activities are not tailored to the individual's interests, cognitive decline accelerates. Answers must reference the nursing home setting for full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Nathaniel is a 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has recently moved into a 20-bed residential care home. Staff are under pressure and do not always read his care plan. He is sometimes given standard meals that do not meet his dietary needs, and he is rarely invited to join group activities because staff assume he prefers to be in his room.

Discuss the effects on Nathaniel's health and wellbeing as a result of person-centred values not being applied. In your answer, make connections between the PIES effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sustained analysis covering multiple PIES areas with clear connections between them. Accurate use of HSC terminology (malnutrition, dehydration, low self-esteem, social withdrawal, etc.). Argument anchored consistently to Nathaniel and the residential care home context. A supported judgement on which effect is most significant and why. Example chain: ignoring dietary needs (absence of individuality) leads to blood sugar instability/malnutrition (P), which causes confusion and loss of concentration (I), leading to low self-esteem and stress (E), which causes Nathaniel to withdraw and feel lonely (S). Judgement: the physical effects are most immediately dangerous because uncontrolled diabetes can be life-threatening, but the emotional and social effects compound the harm and may be hardest to reverse.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most PIES areas covered, generally accurate, mostly applied to Nathaniel and the care home. Some connections between PIES effects attempted. Limited or implicit judgement.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some relevant PIES effects identified, mostly descriptive, limited connections between areas. Some reference to Nathaniel or the setting. No clear judgement.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic PIES points listed without development or connection. Little or no reference to the named service user or setting.

practice_questions.text: Describe two intellectual effects on a service user when person-centred values are not applied.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per intellectual effect, up to 2 marks. Accept: lack of progress or skills development; failure to achieve potential; loss of concentration; lack of mental stimulation. Credit brief description of each effect — a name alone scores the mark, but a name plus a qualifying phrase (e.g. 'loss of concentration because the service user is given no tasks that engage their mind') scores more securely.

practice_questions.text:
Which verbal communication skill means waiting calmly for a service user to express themselves without rushing them?
A) Clarity
B) Volume
C) Patience
D) Team working
practice_questions.marks: C) Patience [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two verbal communication skills a practitioner should use when speaking to a service user.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two correct verbal communication skills from the spec list. Accept: clarity; empathy; patience; appropriate vocabulary; tone; volume; pace; adapting type/method to needs; willingness to contribute to team working.

practice_questions.text: Outline how a care worker at a day centre should adapt their pace when speaking with a service user who has just been given difficult news.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming the adjustment (slow down / speak more slowly / pause between ideas); 1 mark for a reason or brief development (e.g. to give the service user time to process the information; because rushing may cause them to miss key details or feel their distress is being dismissed).

practice_questions.text: Jasmine is a support worker at a community centre running a weekly wellbeing group for adults with mild learning disabilities. Describe how Jasmine should use appropriate vocabulary and empathy when leading a group discussion about healthy eating.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per skill). Appropriate vocabulary (up to 2): names the skill or its application (1) — e.g. uses simple, clear language without jargon; avoids medical terms; speaks at the level of the group; checks understanding regularly; development linking to the community centre context and service users (1) — e.g. saying 'fruit and vegetables' rather than 'five-a-day nutritional requirements' means group members understand and engage rather than switching off. Empathy (up to 2): names the skill or its application (1) — e.g. acknowledges that changing habits can feel hard; reflects back what group members say; development (1) — e.g. by saying 'it sounds like cooking can feel overwhelming when you're tired' Jasmine validates their experience, which means members feel safe to share honestly and are more likely to act on any guidance. Answers must reference the community centre or the group members for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain how using appropriate verbal communication skills benefits service users in a GP surgery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation covering two or more verbal communication skills with developed reasoning for each. Argument clearly anchored to the GP surgery setting throughout. Uses connective language (because, therefore, this means that). Example: 'A GP who uses clarity when explaining a diagnosis avoids medical jargon, which means the patient understands their condition and can make an informed decision about treatment (benefit: empowerment). If the GP also shows empathy by acknowledging how worrying a new diagnosis can be, the patient feels valued and is more likely to open up about symptoms they might otherwise not have mentioned, which improves the accuracy of care.' At least two such chains expected, with reference to specific service user benefits (reassurance, feeling valued, trust, well-informed, empowerment).

Secure (3-4 marks): Most relevant skills named with mostly accurate explanation. Generally anchored to the GP surgery. Some connective language used. Benefits identified but not always fully developed.

Developing (1-2 marks): Some relevant verbal skills named. Limited explanation. May list skills without developing reasons or benefits. Little connection to the GP surgery setting.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a practitioner's willingness to contribute to team working supports the care of service users in a nursing home.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing a team communication behaviour (e.g. sharing observations at handover; raising concerns with a line manager; contributing to care plan meetings; flagging changes in a service user's condition). 1 mark for linking to the service user's care (e.g. this means all staff are informed and can provide consistent care; errors and omissions in care are less likely; the service user's needs are met even when different staff are on shift).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the six active listening skills named in the spec?
A) Using appropriate vocabulary
B) Adjusting volume
C) Summarising key points
D) Using medical jargon
practice_questions.marks: C) Summarising key points [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one non-verbal communication skill a practitioner should use when speaking with a service user.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any correct non-verbal skill. Accept: eye contact; facial expressions; gestures; positioning (space/height/personal space); positive body language/no crossed arms; sense of humour. Do not accept verbal skills such as tone or pace.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'reflecting feelings' as an active listening skill.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic description (e.g. repeating or acknowledging what the service user has said about their feelings); 1 mark for development or example (e.g. by saying back to the service user what they appear to be feeling, such as 'it sounds like you are worried about your appointment', the practitioner shows they have understood and encourages the service user to continue).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a practitioner in a walk-in centre should use eye contact and positioning when speaking with a service user who is anxious about a minor procedure.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per skill). Eye contact (up to 2): describes appropriate use (1) — e.g. maintains a warm, steady eye contact rather than looking away or checking notes; development (1) — this shows the service user the practitioner is focused on them, which reduces anxiety and helps the service user feel their concerns are being taken seriously. Positioning (up to 2): describes appropriate positioning (1) — e.g. sits at the same level/height as the service user, at a comfortable distance that respects personal space; development (1) — being at the same height removes the sense of a power imbalance and makes the service user feel equal and respected, which is particularly important for a service user who is already anxious. Both answers must be linked to the walk-in centre context or the service user's anxiety for full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Suki is a health care assistant at a 40-bed NHS hospital ward. She is speaking with Darnell, a 25-year-old patient who has been told he will need to stay in hospital for several days following a diagnosis of a serious infection. Darnell is distressed and struggling to explain his concerns clearly.

Explain how Suki could use active listening skills to support Darnell during this conversation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Explains at least three specific active listening skills by name. Each skill linked with a reason (because/therefore/this means that) and anchored to Darnell's distress and the hospital setting. Example chains: 'Suki maintains an open, relaxed posture (skill) because crossed arms or a tense stance would signal she is uncomfortable or in a hurry; this means Darnell feels she is fully present and safe to speak' / 'Suki reflects Darnell's feelings — for example, saying “It sounds like you’re really worried about being away from home” (skill) because this shows she has heard and understood his emotional state; Darnell feels valued rather than dismissed, which encourages him to share the full picture of his concerns' / 'Suki summarises at the end of the conversation, reviewing the key points Darnell has raised (skill), which confirms she has understood correctly and prevents misunderstanding about what will happen next'. Judgement or conclusion not required for 6-mark, but expected for 8-mark.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two or more active listening skills named with explanation. Generally linked to Darnell or the hospital ward. Uses some connective language. Benefits identified.

Developing (1-2 marks): One active listening skill named, or general statements about listening without naming specific behaviours. Little connection to the named service user or setting.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which positive body language supports communication with a service user in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per way, up to 2 marks. Accept: no crossed arms means the service user does not interpret the posture as defensive or impatient (1); facing the service user with an open stance signals engagement and willingness to listen (1); using an appropriate sense of humour can reduce tension and make the service user feel more comfortable (1). Brief description of each — a named behaviour alone scores 1 mark; a named behaviour with a development or reason scores more securely.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the role of an advocate in a health and social care setting?
A) A person who translates between two different languages
B) A person who uses Braille to support a visually impaired service user
C) A person who speaks on behalf of a service user and represents their wishes
D) A person who uses voice activated software on behalf of a service user
practice_questions.marks: C) A person who speaks on behalf of a service user and represents their wishes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two special methods of communication that may be used in a health and social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two correct special methods from the spec list. Accept: advocate; Braille; British Sign Language/BSL; interpreters; Makaton; voice activated software.

practice_questions.text: Outline how Braille supports a service user with a visual impairment in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing what Braille is or how it is used (e.g. a system of raised dots read by touch, used to produce written information such as appointment letters, consent forms or activity schedules in a format a visually impaired person can read independently). 1 mark for a benefit or development (e.g. this means the service user can access written information without relying on a sighted person to read it for them, supporting their independence and right to equal treatment).

practice_questions.text: Describe how using Makaton and an interpreter could support two different service users at a day centre.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per method). Makaton (up to 2): describes the method accurately (1) — Makaton uses signs and symbols alongside speech for service users with learning difficulties or communication disorders; application to a service user and the day centre (1) — e.g. a member of staff uses simple Makaton signs when offering a choice of activity to a service user with a severe learning disability, meaning the service user can communicate their preference and exercise their right to choice. Interpreter (up to 2): describes the method accurately (1) — an interpreter translates spoken communication between two parties who do not share a language; application to a service user and the day centre (1) — e.g. when a newly arrived service user speaks no English, a professional telephone interpreter is arranged for their care plan meeting, meaning the service user can accurately explain their needs and the practitioner understands them correctly. Answers must refer to the day centre context or a named service user for full marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain how using British Sign Language and voice activated software could support service users in a health and social care setting to communicate effectively.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Explains both methods with developed reasoning, linked clearly to service user benefits and the care setting. Uses connective language throughout. Example: 'British Sign Language is a complete visual language used by many Deaf people (method). In a hospital setting, a Deaf patient may not be able to understand spoken explanations of their diagnosis or treatment, because BSL is their first language and standard spoken communication is inaccessible to them. If a qualified BSL interpreter is provided for the appointment, the patient can ask questions and give informed consent (benefit: right to information and right to choice). Without this, there is a risk of misunderstanding that could harm the patient.' / 'Voice activated software allows a person with a physical disability, such as motor neurone disease, to control their device using spoken commands (method). This means they can access information, communicate with others and manage their daily activities independently, without relying on a care worker for every task (benefit: independence and empowerment). This upholds the person-centred value of independence, as the service user retains control over aspects of their own life.'

Secure (3-4 marks): Both methods addressed, mostly accurate. Generally linked to service user benefits and a care setting. Some connective language. Benefits identified.

Developing (1-2 marks): One method addressed with limited explanation, or both named with no development. Little connection to service users or the care setting.

practice_questions.text: Describe one difference between an advocate and an interpreter.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for accurately describing the advocate's role (speaks on behalf of a service user, representing their wishes and rights when they cannot do so for themselves). 1 mark for accurately describing the interpreter's role (translates spoken communication between parties who speak different languages, without adding their own views). Both marks require accurate descriptions that highlight the distinction — a correct description of one role alone scores 1 mark.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an impact of poor communication in a care setting?
A) Service users feel empowered to make choices
B) Service users feel valued and respected
C) Service users may misunderstand information if it is not clearly explained
D) Service users are well informed about their care
practice_questions.marks: C) Service users may misunderstand information if it is not clearly explained [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by using appropriate vocabulary in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that appropriate vocabulary means using language the service user can understand; 1 mark for developing this, for example by noting that jargon or medical terms should be avoided so the service user is not confused or excluded from understanding their own care.

practice_questions.text: Describe two impacts of poor communication on a service user in a health or social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each impact clearly described, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: misunderstanding because information is not clearly explained; errors or danger to health due to inaccurate record keeping or unclear handover; distress or upset if the service user feels patronised by over-simplified language; failure to take in information if speech is delivered too fast. A one-word answer without description earns 0. Each mark requires the name of the impact plus a characteristic or consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain why inaccurate record keeping is a risk to service users in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that inaccurate record keeping means information about a service user's care is recorded incorrectly or incompletely; 1 mark for explaining why this is caused by or linked to poor communication (e.g. unclear verbal handover, failure to document a change in condition); 1 mark for explaining the consequence using 'because' or 'therefore' (e.g. therefore a practitioner may administer the wrong medication or miss a critical change in the service user's health, putting them in danger). No third mark without reasoning chain.

practice_questions.text:
Sanya is a support worker at a day centre for adults with learning disabilities. She has noticed that one service user, 24-year-old Marcus, often looks confused after receiving information from the visiting health coordinator. The health coordinator tends to use medical terminology and speaks quickly during appointments.

Describe four ways in which the health coordinator could improve their communication to better meet Marcus's needs at the day centre.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described improvement, up to 4 marks. Acceptable answers include: using simple, plain language free from medical jargon so Marcus can understand; slowing the pace of speech to give Marcus time to process information; checking Marcus's understanding by asking him to explain back what he has understood; using visual supports such as pictures or written summaries alongside speech; using active listening behaviours (nodding, maintaining eye contact) to encourage Marcus to ask questions; giving Marcus time to respond without rushing. Answers that name an improvement without describing it earn 0 marks each. Answers that merely say 'communicate better' or 'be clearer' without specifying how earn 0.

practice_questions.text:
A residential care home manager is reviewing communication practices after a service user raised a complaint about feeling patronised and uninformed during their care. The manager must decide whether to invest in staff communication training or whether the existing guidelines are sufficient.

Discuss the importance of effective communication in health and social care settings, and evaluate the impact that poor communication can have on service users.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Response discusses both the importance of effective communication AND the impact of poor communication with sustained application to a named care setting and service user type. Uses precise HSC terminology throughout (empowerment, trust, person-centred values, right to choice/confidentiality, PIES impacts). Builds clear chains of reasoning linking a communication skill (or failure) to an outcome (right, value, PIES effect). Offers a balanced discussion with a supported evaluative judgement (e.g. comparing the relative harm of different poor communication impacts, or judging whether training would address the root causes).

Secure (5-6 marks): Covers both effective and poor communication with mostly accurate application to the scenario. Uses some HSC terminology correctly. Most points are developed with a 'because' or 'therefore' chain. May be slightly one-sided or lack a final evaluative judgement.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points present but limited development. May address only one side (e.g. only good communication). Some attempt to apply to a care setting. Points stated rather than analysed.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about communication with little or no application to a named setting, service user, or rights and values framework. Listing without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what a standard DBS check reveals?
A) Spent and unspent convictions plus any information held by local police
B) Only unspent convictions
C) Spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings
D) Whether a person is on the barred list
practice_questions.marks: C) Spent and unspent convictions, cautions, reprimands and warnings [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two groups of people who may need safeguarding in health and social care settings.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each group named with a brief reason or characteristic, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: children (may not recognise harm or be unable to report it); older adults in residential care (dependent on carers, may have limited capacity to raise concerns); people with physical or learning disabilities (may have difficulty communicating concerns); people with mental health conditions (may have reduced capacity at times or accounts may be questioned); people with sensory impairment such as sight or hearing loss (limited access to information or support); homeless people (precarious circumstances, limited access to formal support). A one-word group name without any characteristic earns 0.

practice_questions.text: Describe two emotional impacts on a service user when safeguarding is not in place.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described emotional impact, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: depression or persistent low mood; low self-esteem or feeling worthless or inadequate; anxiety or fear; distress and upset; anger or frustration; feeling unable to trust adults or practitioners. A single word (e.g. 'sad') without description of characteristics earns 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain why safeguarding training is important for all staff in a residential care home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that training ensures all staff know the signs of harm; 1 mark for explaining why this matters (e.g. because any staff member may be the first person a service user chooses to disclose to, so all staff need to know the reporting procedure); 1 mark for explaining the outcome with a 'therefore' or 'this means that' chain (e.g. therefore concerns are reported quickly and consistently, reducing the risk of ongoing harm to the service user). No third mark without reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Priya manages a 20-place residential care home for adults with learning disabilities. A new care worker, 22-year-old Tomasz, has just started on the support team. The setting also works with volunteers who help with activities twice a week.

Describe four safeguarding procedures the residential care home should have in place to protect its service users.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described procedure, up to 4 marks. Acceptable answers include: a safeguarding policy setting out responsibilities, reporting pathways and what staff should do if they have a concern; a named Designated Safeguarding Lead to receive and coordinate concerns; safeguarding training for all staff (including new starters like Tomasz) so they can recognise signs of harm and know reporting routes; DBS checks (enhanced with barred list) completed before Tomasz or any volunteer begins work with service users. Answers that name a procedure without describing what it does earn 0 for that mark.

practice_questions.text:
A children's charity runs an after-school club and Saturday sports programme at a community centre. The club has 30 children aged 7-11 including some with physical disabilities and one child whose parent has recently raised a concern about unexplained bruising.

Discuss the importance of safeguarding procedures in the children's charity's setting, and evaluate how effectively these procedures protect the children in the club.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Response discusses the importance of each safeguarding procedure (policy, DSL, training, DBS) with clear reasoning about why each is necessary in the named setting. Applies to the specific vulnerabilities of the service users (children, some with disabilities). Analyses the impacts of inadequate safeguarding using PIES with at least one connection between categories. Reaches an evaluative judgement, for example weighing whether procedures alone are sufficient or whether staff culture and training quality also matter. Uses precise terminology (safeguarding policy, DSL, standard/enhanced DBS, barred list, duty to report, disclosure).

Secure (5-6 marks): Covers most procedures with mostly accurate application. Refers to the named setting and the specific vulnerability of children. Some PIES analysis of impacts. Mostly developed points. May lack a final judgement or have one under-developed PIES connection.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content about safeguarding procedures but limited development. May list procedures without explaining their importance. Limited or no PIES analysis. Some reference to the scenario.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic knowledge about safeguarding with little or no application to a named setting, vulnerable group, or procedural framework. Listing rather than discussing or evaluating.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a personal hygiene measure in a care setting?
A) Mopping floors daily
B) Disposing of clinical waste in colour-coded bags
C) Wearing a disposable apron
D) Tying hair back before giving personal care
practice_questions.marks: D) Tying hair back before giving personal care [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two types of PPE that a healthcare assistant on a hospital ward should use when providing personal care.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each type of PPE named with a brief description of its purpose, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: disposable gloves (worn to prevent contact with bodily fluids or skin); disposable aprons (worn to protect clothing and prevent cross-contamination); face mask (worn to prevent respiratory droplet transmission). A PPE name without any description of purpose earns 0 for that mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two general cleanliness measures a children's nursery should carry out to reduce the risk of infection spreading.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each measure clearly described with relevant characteristics, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: cleaning and disinfecting toys and play equipment regularly because children put items in their mouths; using anti-bacterial spray on surfaces such as tables and door handles to kill bacteria; mopping floors and vacuuming carpets daily to reduce bacteria and allergens; cleaning and disinfecting toilets frequently to prevent the spread of gastrointestinal infections; correct disposal of hazardous waste such as soiled nappies or first aid materials. A measure named without description earns 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important for care workers in a residential home to avoid wearing jewellery at work.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that jewellery can harbour bacteria in hard-to-clean areas (e.g. under rings, around clasps); 1 mark for explaining the connection to infection risk (e.g. because bacteria accumulated under rings cannot be removed by handwashing alone, meaning the care worker may pass pathogens to a service user during personal care); 1 mark for explaining the consequence for the service user (e.g. therefore residents, who may be elderly and immunocompromised, are at greater risk of infection that could seriously harm their health). No third mark without a 'because'/'therefore' reasoning chain.

practice_questions.text:
Fatoumata is a kitchen assistant at a 35-bed nursing home. She prepares and serves meals to residents, some of whom have compromised immune systems. Her manager has asked her to review her infection prevention practice.

Describe four infection prevention measures Fatoumata should follow in her role at the nursing home.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described measure relevant to Fatoumata's role in food preparation and serving, up to 4 marks. Acceptable answers include: tying hair back or wearing a hairnet to prevent hair from falling into food; wearing disposable gloves when handling food to prevent contact contamination; wearing a disposable apron over clothing to prevent transferring micro-organisms from clothing to food or service users; following the correct hand washing routine before food preparation and after handling waste; wearing no jewellery (especially rings) so bacteria cannot accumulate in hard-to-clean areas; regularly cleaning and disinfecting food preparation surfaces using anti-bacterial sprays; correctly disposing of food waste or soiled disposable items. Answers must describe the measure, not just name it, to earn the mark.

practice_questions.text:
A community health visitor carries out home visits to support new parents and their babies. She visits 10 families a day and travels between homes throughout the working day.

Explain the importance of infection prevention measures the health visitor should follow to protect herself and the babies she visits.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Response explains at least three infection prevention measures with clear chains of reasoning using 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that'. Applies each measure to the specific context (home visits, babies, multiple households). Uses accurate terminology (PPE, personal hygiene, general cleanliness, disposable aprons/gloves, handwashing). Explains why babies are particularly at risk and why the multi-household nature of the role increases transmission risk. Two or three well-developed points rather than a list of brief points.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two or three measures explained with some reasoning. Mostly accurate application to the named context. Some use of 'because' or 'therefore'. May lack one reasoning chain or have limited development.

Developing (2 marks): Relevant measures identified with limited explanation. Points stated rather than explained. Limited or no 'because' chain.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic point about infection prevention with no reasoning or application to the named context.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a safety measure rather than a safety procedure?
A) Carrying out a risk assessment before a group outing
B) Conducting a monthly fire drill
C) Placing a wet floor sign after mopping a corridor
D) Training all staff in moving and handling techniques
practice_questions.marks: C) Placing a wet floor sign after mopping a corridor [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two security measures a residential care home could use to control who enters the building.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each security measure named with a brief description of how it controls access, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: electronic swipe card entry system (only authorised staff can open doors); buzzer entry system (visitors must be approved by staff before entering); security pad with pin code (restricts access to certain areas); signing-in and out book for visitors (records who is on the premises); staff member monitoring entrance (prevents unauthorised access at the door). Measure name without description earns 0.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why monitoring of keys is an important security measure in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described reason, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: limiting the number of keyholders reduces the risk of keys being lost or misused; a keyholder list means the setting always knows who has access to restricted areas; key monitoring restricts access to medication stores or equipment rooms to authorised staff only; in settings with vulnerable service users (e.g. adults with dementia), key monitoring prevents residents from leaving unsupervised. Each mark requires a characteristic or consequence, not just 'to keep people safe'.

practice_questions.text: Explain why risk assessments are an important safety procedure in health and social care settings.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that a risk assessment involves identifying hazards and evaluating the likelihood and severity of harm; 1 mark for explaining why this matters using 'because' or 'therefore' (e.g. because hazards that are not identified cannot be controlled, meaning staff or service users may be harmed unnecessarily); 1 mark for explaining the outcome for service users or staff (e.g. therefore carrying out a risk assessment before an activity means controls are in place to reduce risk, protecting both service users and staff from preventable injury). No third mark without a reasoning chain.

practice_questions.text:
Kevin is the registered manager of a supported living house for four adults with learning disabilities. The house has an open-plan ground floor and a garden. Kevin is reviewing safety and security arrangements following feedback from a recent inspection.

Describe four safety procedures or security measures Kevin should ensure are in place at the supported living house.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly described safety procedure or security measure relevant to the named setting, up to 4 marks. Acceptable answers include: a first aid policy setting out who is the trained first aider and where equipment is stored; a fire drill carried out regularly so all staff and residents know the evacuation procedure and assembly point; a risk assessment for garden activities or the use of any household equipment; staff training in moving and handling to ensure residents are supported safely; an electronic swipe card or buzzer entry system on the front door to prevent unauthorised access; a signing-in book for all visitors so Kevin knows who is on the premises at any time; window locks on upstairs windows to prevent falls; key monitoring with a keyholder list to restrict access to medication storage. Do not accept 'have CCTV' as this is not listed in the spec content for 4.3/4.4. Each mark requires a description, not just a name.

practice_questions.text:
A GP surgery serves a mixed population including elderly patients, young children and adults with mental health conditions. The practice manager is reviewing both safety and security arrangements at the surgery.

Discuss the importance of safety procedures, safety measures and security measures in a health or social care setting, and evaluate how effectively they protect service users and staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Response discusses safety procedures, safety measures AND security measures with clear distinction between the first two. Applies at least three examples from the spec content to the named setting (GP surgery) with reference to the specific service user groups (elderly, children, mental health). Builds chains of reasoning linking each procedure or measure to a specific protection outcome. Reaches an evaluative judgement, for example evaluating whether procedures (which require training and commitment from all staff) are harder to maintain than measures (which are physical and automatic), or considering the balance between security and service users' rights (e.g. locked doors may feel restrictive but protect vulnerable patients). Uses precise terminology throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): Covers most categories with mostly accurate application to the named setting. Uses some precise terminology. Points are mostly developed. May lack a fully supported evaluative judgement or one well-developed chain of reasoning.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content but limited development. May conflate procedures and measures. Limited application to the named setting. Points stated rather than analysed.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about safety or security with little or no application to the GP surgery or the specific service user groups. Listing rather than discussing or evaluating.
